cues.t: Hello, this is James D’ Angelo. Today we are going to be jumping into a question that we discovered in democracy perhaps even a really big flaw with how American democracy
is administered. And because the midterm elections are coming up and this is so important for ideas particularly with Congress, we are going to try to get
this done by then. And the beauty of this is even though we see this fundamental flaw with democracy, one that is at the root of almost every problem in American society today,
the reform is ridiculously cheap. In fact, we believe that all the problems that we run into can be solved with one single cardboard box. It sounds completely preposterous
but hang in there because this is really easy to understand but it is really outrageous stuff. So when I was originally developing this video
a few weeks ago, I called the video “Something Happened in the 70’s” because almost everywhere
I was looking from economists to politicians to newspapers to journals, people were pointing
their fingers at some mysterious event that happened sometime in the 70’s that precipitated
an enormous amount of problems with our economy, our government and even our social institutions.
And because this moment is so crucial, I’m going to run quickly through most of these encounters that I was having. So let’s get started.
Here we’ve got a Wikipedia article on the Golden Age of Capitalism which it considers to be from 1945 to the mid 1970’s. It says, “Following the end of World War II, in 1945,
the Golden Age of Capitalism lasted until the early 70’s.” Paul Krugman pinpoints this massive rise in debt leading up to the financial crisis to
sometime here in the early 70’s. Joseph Stiglitz another Nobel Laureate, talks about the beginning of government regulation decay.
You’ve got Paul Ryan and other Republicans pointing a finger at this time for this massive increase in government expenditure. You have Libertarian Ron Paul talking about
increase in government regulations that makes it more difficult for a free market to do its thing. You have the scholar Lawrence Lessig who points
his finger at campaign funding and he finds the date 1974 very intriguing. “From 1974
to 2008, the average amount it took to run for re-election to the House went from $56,000 to more than $1.3 million.” So he found this problem but he didn’t find the cause.
He did not find the root. So here’s Robert Reich at U Cal Berkeley, and talks about the great prosperity that began in 1947 and continued in his term until
1977. And he focuses on this. I mean, this is a big graphic for him. How inequality was at its highest here in the 70’s and then just started to drop, basically, the rich
getting much, much richer; the poor, middle class losing out. He said, “Starting in the mid-70’s a vicious cycle occurred which created a flattening of wages, rising debt
and enormous income inequality.” Here’s Elizabeth Warren who focuses also on flattening of wages, in particular, males’ wages which began in 1970 and has been flat
ever since. And she also focuses on, what Stiglitz was looking at, this change in regulations,
these very peculiar changes that seem to focus on assisting the wealthy.
Everyone’s heard of the massive increase in executives’ pay. Here’s a graph showing that. You can see that scorching up and making a big turn also in the 70’s.
And here we have Thomas Piketty who is a big celebrity this year because of his book called,
“Capital,” which looks at how wealth keeps getting wealthier just by itself without any action whatsoever, and this is leading to a brand new Gilded Age.
He too, looks at the 1970’s as the lowest point of inequality and then sort of a scorching rise, a scorching rise, not something that’s kind of delayed and slow; something immediately
starts jumping up. And you have all these other funny things that happen. The church starts marching into Washington, D.C., to pay the lobbyists to
do their thing. You can see this happening right here. Where it sort of takes a turn, a sharp turn in the 70’s and then shoots up like a rocket.
And almost every where you turn. Here we have incarceration of Americans. Okay so it increases
for a while and then starts shooting up like crazy.
We have this concept of the 1 percenters or even the 0.01 percenters. Everything seems to be pretty good, in fact, going towards more equality until sometime here in the 70’s
and again, like everything else it’s shooting up.
It’s really ironic to think that the Republicans who have been presidents since the 70’s and their struggles to lower government spending. Here’s a chart about the slowest increases
in government spending since the 70’s and its not Reagan, it’s not Bush, Clinton did a pretty good job, Obama did a pretty good job.
So, even though Ronald Reagan and George Bush believed wholeheartedly and really tried to lower government spending they were having a really hard time doing that.
And everywhere I was turning, I was seeing something happening. Union membership in the United States. Here we are 1970’s and it starts shooting down. Looks like it’s kind
of like at a peak over here but it’s fairly random fluctuation but then the shooting down happens over here. And what you are seeing here is really the development of unions.
So, the whole idea of unions really takes off over here, everything seems to be going fairly
flat and then - BOOM - they collapse. Okay, and remember unions are very important at this idea of separation of powers. Unions are one form of power. We have the
corporate leadership, government and other types of power. So, with the decline of unions means
that we are losing one form of our separation of powers.
And as we spoke about in the previous slide, we may even be losing another form. Presidents
are finding themselves more ineffectual than they used to be. And partly because of this, confidence in government over the last 30 to 40 years has fallen dramatically.
Here, Vietnam was going on, race riots were happening in the 60’s, all these seemingly
big government problems but you still have a lot of confidence in Congress and you have a lot of confidence in government in general. And this starts shooting down.
It doesn’t take a smooth slope. But here we are today; we have a 7% confidence in government
when in the 70’s you have 40%. These next couple of charts are pretty interesting.
This increase of complexity. It’s actually a very terrifying increase, that also took a sharp turn in the 70’s and has been growing like a rocket ship ever since.
These charts in particular are looking at the tax code. So if you’re just going to do your taxes and you have to understand how taxes work. Well, there are more and more pages
of things you have to understand. All these little lines that might be giving benefits to different groups, okay, these lines just keep adding up and they’ve been increasing.
But this is not the only increase in complexity. We're seeing it everywhere. Okay, so just when Congress
is going to vote on a bill, the bills themselves are growing enormously. Here, it’s kind
of interesting to think about the Bill of Rights. This is our entire Bill of Rights.
Here’s Article 1 of our Bill of Rights. All articles, fundamental things about our democracy, that you can fit all on one page. Well, current bills are not like that at all.
And this enormous growth in the size of the bills really started to happen right around 1970. And here it’s discussed in kind of a humorous
way, where each congressman, each year used to have to read slightly more than 2,000 pages of legislation a year. And, that number in 2006 has now shot up to 7,000 pages of legislation.
Legislation is not easy to read. And there’s no congressman that can end up reading it all. And all of this stuff, starting in the 70’s
leads to this really outrageous, really terrifying conclusion that came out this year. Okay,
so this guy right here, who is the main researcher, is named Gilens, and this is his buddy Benjamin Page. And they released a paper this year with this
graph that we are going to be focusing on throughout the entire video. And this graph right here is really a measure of all of democracy and whether democracy is working or not. And
they’ve been with John Stewart. They’ve been all over the place, just with this one graph. And what they did, was they focused on how average
citizens felt about policy and how economic elites felt about the same policy being passed by Congress. And the terrifying thing they found was this flat line. And we’re going
to explain that flat line right now. This is a terrifying line.
What this means is that if the average people, you go out and poll the average citizens, if they feel strongly against a particular bill that’s being proposed in Congress, it
will register down here. Alright, so five percent of the average citizens are for the bill, 95% of the average citizens are against the bill. What are the chances of that bill
getting passed? Well, what they found, was that it was about 30%.
Now the opposite. So if most of the people on the street, you poll them, they're very excited about a particular bill, they really want it to happen, what are the odds if most
Americans, the overwhelming majority of Americans want a particular bill to be passed, what
are the odds of that bill passing? That was also 30%. This is terrifying.
What this means is no matter what average citizens feel there is no change in whether Congress is likely to pass the bill. Congress is unaffected by the average citizen. This
is powerful stuff. This is new stuff. Okay, we didn’t have this data before. The opposite though seems to be happening with the rich. If the economic elites, or the wealthy, are
really in favor of a particular bill, the odds of that bill passing go up dramatically to 60%. If the economic elites are really against a bill passing, it drops to almost
zero. Really what this says is that, it’s easier to reject a bill, to stop a bill in Congress than, to actually pass a bill. But it also
says, money changes Congress. Rich people do get their say in Congress. And the average
citizen, all together, does not affect policy at all.
This is enormous stuff. And, what it means is actually kind of chilling. So if you are someone like
Ron Paul, what this line right here suggests, is that Libertarians are right.
Government never does anything that respects the people. It’s just acting on its own.
It’s raising money for itself. It’s making rich people wealthier.
This is really the first and biggest factual support I’ve seen of Libertarianism in my life. If you are Libertarian, this is virtual proof that you’ve been right. And that all the left
and all the moderate right have been wrong. Okay. Policy does not reflect the will of the people. It seems likely that since Tocqueville published
his book over a hundred years ago, we haven’t had a better critique of democracy. And we have to start thinking about flashing a little “TYRANNY ALERT” button.
Economic elites control this “democracy”. So if you are measuring democracy and democracy is responding to the people, this line for the average citizen needs to be somewhere
around here. I suspect that in some countries it may actually be the other way. So it’s even worse. So if you have a dictator, who is getting
everything they want, almost all the laws that are passed are going to be completely against the peoples’ wishes. So almost, negative. This is sort of a terrible dictator,
this line right here is sort of the ideal. Right the now the U.S. government is at this terrible state which just says we don’t care about the people at all. They don’t
influence decision at all; very big problem. Okay, and so if all these government policies
are now reflecting the wishes of the wealthy well then we should see more wealth. And we should see more poverty. You get lots and lots of books claiming this, but they don’t
see the cause. So here you have this “Age of Greed”, “The triumph of finance, and the decline of America from 1970 to the present.” So,
once again we see the 70’s. And have some people suggested without knowing exactly where or how that our democracy has been hacked. Okay, so this great thing the founders had
developed is actually been tweaked in some way so that it’s now benefitting only very
small numbers of people. So, here we have a problem. We have lots of smoke. All these economists, all the politicians are clearly analyzing the problem but we don’t
know the source. Okay so there’s a lot of smoke. Everybody pointing to the 70’s knows that there is a problem. But where is the fire?
And, we keep hearing the same things. “Well, people are greedy. Bankers are bad. Government
is corrupt. Money is evil. You’ll never be able to change any of this.” Here is Jonathan Rauch in his book, Demosclerosis. And as he suggests, and he is absolutely right,
you have liberals blaming conservatives, conservatives blaming the liberals.
You have populists and business bashers blaming money. And then you have the public, the general
public, blaming leadership and then the lack of it. And then as he suggests, there are grounds to believe that none of the above fully comprehend what is going on. And that’s
really been the problem. We all have something to blame but we have not found the common cause. And so, we really have to be looking for this common cause.
This is something that I’ve focused on now for a number of years.
And when I was looking at the graphs I started to see something that I recognize from my experiences in Biology and in Physics. Okay, you see something that grows out of nowhere,
grows exponentially right away, you have a system that has been influenced by some impulse.
Something has been pushed into the system that changed everything.
Here’s a graph of the growth of the Chinese Privet in the South; Southern U.S. It was introduced sometime around here not the 70’s, a little bit earlier and it just took off.
It kind of, looks like some of the graphs that we are looking at.
Here we have the introduction of the Mongoose, the drop of the Skinks, all similar graphs.
And this is the standard S-curve, things that I talk about a lot. You have this lag phase, when something gets introduced. Then you have this rapid growth phase and then you have
a peak. It’s not clear if we reached a peak. The wealthy getting richer; inequality is growing even as we speak. But if we think scientifically,
we have to think that there was some impulse, some change here that led to all of this.
Because it just would be completely unusual that all these different things would take off in the 70’s for different reasons, there must be something that was introduced in the
system that created these problems. If you go down to the Florida Keys and talk about invasive species, one of the colourful ones is the Lionfish which has been multiplying
like crazy in the waters near the Gulf. What we are trying to do is we are trying to find this invasive species that has changed all of government. We’ll call it a search
for our lionfish - our Lionfish of the 1970’s. So I started to focus and direct my attention
to something that happened in the 70’s; tried to find this invasive species. At the time I started to focus on this idea, I was living in Africa. It’s a phenomenal place.
You really get a different view of how democracy works. You really get a different view of how almost everything works. My wife is Ugandan. I love Africa.
But while I was there from 2008 to 2012, there were a number of elections. There was a very
famous one in Kenya which led to a lot of violence, and then the the follow-up elections, and all that. Every time these elections came about, the
government was complaining that they might not have enough money to run the elections.
When I first saw this, it caught me by surprise. I never considered the cost of running an election. And indeed, it’s pretty expensive. You have to set up all the voting booths.
You need security. You have to print the ballots and you have to organize the whole system.
These are very expensive undertakings. But this did not mean that elections in the developed world were cheap. Here we have an article from UK complaining about the price
of running these elections. It turns out they’re very, very expensive.
Being in Africa, I started to think about, wow they all got these cell phones now, what if we can do some form of e-voting, electronic voting. I started to look at the tech of trying
to solve this problem. Here are some great graphics of people getting all excited about voting electronically. You have companies that are developing electronic
voting systems. The dream is everyone could just wake up on Election Day, get their hands on a phone, and they could just vote. That’s when I started really banging my
head with some of these problems that I never really considered about democracy. And I ran into the million dollar question. Here we have this lady. She’s stepping out
from a curtain. She’s inside a voting booth put up by the state so that she can vote.
I was going to replace this with someone voting at home on the phone. I really had to start
to think about why we needed voting booths. This pushed me harder into something that I even held more dear. I am a big fan of transparency. Transparency in government, all the transparency
you can get. I always thought more transparency the better until I started to jump into this.
The question that I started to face was, “Can we get too much of a good thing?” Are there situations where you have too much transparency and it actually starts to put things at risk?
And the answer is, yes. Really the only place where transparency becomes a problem is when it comes to voting. There are two huge problems where transparency confronts
head on democracy and the ability to vote. And if you are a democracy expert, someone who is into this stuff, pause the video and see if you can think about these two major
problems; because these two major problems change the game. They really need to be understood
so we can understand transparency, elections and democracy.
For those of you who don’t feel like pausing, we’re jumping forward.
The first big problem and this is under the headline, ELECTORAL FRAUD. Problem 1 is the idea of INTIMIDATION. Let’s think about this for a second.
Say, you’re voting at home and the issue is on domestic violence, and if you are polling women in the street, most of them are for this bill and for putting all these perpetrators
into jail. But at home, what you have is the guy is sitting there and the woman sitting there and she might be voting right in front of the guy; right in front of the guy who
is beating her. Is she as likely to vote for this bill that would put the perpetrator in jail or is she more likely to vote “no” because he’s
sitting right there, willing to punch her? This is a major problem. If someone’s voting, it’s very hard for them to vote their conscience if someone is sitting over them watching them
vote. They can be intimidated. So it’s very hard to imagine voting at home with issues like domestic violence or some sort of control that affects these families
at home. But you have to think that some people might be forced to vote from their business.
The boss of the business might insists that he is watching as they are voting or he might even somehow figure out some way to get a hold of their phone and do the voting himself.
This is dangerous stuff. This is a common and well-known problem, been known for thousands of years, this idea of intimidation. We can take it one further,
because this really happened in the United States. A lot of the voting before 1890 was done where the person walked into a courthouse and say who they were voting for. The people
recognized all the people in town and the townspeople would come in and say who they’re voting for. The deputies or the people working for the
town were there writing down the votes. A lot of times you might even have the sheriff there making sure the votes are done well; making sure that everything is conducted well.
But you have a problem here, right? What if you’re voting for the sheriff. Now, the sheriff is watching you vote for him or not vote for him. Say you don’t like the
sheriff. Say you think someone else should be in his position. But say he is likely to win, are you going to stand in front of him and say “No I won’t vote for him” or
“I’m voting for the other guy” knowing full well that you might need the sheriff in a few weeks to help you with the situation at your ranch.
If you voted against him, and then you call him and say, “Look, I need help, sheriff.
I need help. There’s a real problem here. Someone is stealing stuff from my bar.” Is the sheriff as likely to come? Just by vocalizing your vote, by being public
about your vote, you set yourself up for some situation where intimidation could happen.
And so you get a lot of incumbency power based on this one concept of electoral fraud, called
intimidation. It’s really easy to think of myriad ways where intimidation can happen. So that’s problem 1, intimidation.
The other problem is just as big. It is the other big reason why you need voting booths.
And the other problem is VOTE BUYING. Most Americans, we don’t even think about it anymore. Since the 1890’s there’s been voting booths mostly everywhere. We open the
curtain and have some private situation and we vote.
But it turns out that studies on voting buying, show vote buying from the beginning of our democracy all the way up until the mid 1930’s was rife. Some studies suggest that in the
1930’s, where they didn’t have secret ballots. Over 5% of the population was being paid to vote a certain way. Most of us just don’t think much about vote
buying, but it is because of vote buying that you will never get a receipt when you vote.
This is something you have never seen before or you have never been handed, some sort of notary has now said that you’ve just voted for Ron Paul.
You’ve walked out of the voting booth and you now have proof of how you voted not only for the president but maybe for all these local elections. This has never happened to
you. And there is a reason for that. This has been studied and understood perfectly.
If you can show how you voted it is much, much easier to sell your vote. Imagine a guy
who runs up to all these kind of homeless guys or guys who need food or something like that and he says, “I’ll give you 20 bucks for every receipt that shows that you voted
for me”. This has real value; the ability to sell a vote. If someone votes in a voting booth and is not handed a receipt suddenly they can’t
prove that they voted and it makes it much harder for the guy with a lot of money to show up to these guys and say, “Hey, I want you to go over there and vote for me”. All
of a sudden the value of their vote goes down in price because they have nothing to sell.
Because he can pay these guys to go to the voting booth, but in the privacy of the voting booth, they can vote against him. They can take the money and they can vote against him.
So, the value and ability to sell their votes goes down almost entirely if they cannot prove
how they voted. So, the ability to prove how you voted really increases your ability to sell your vote. So if you are going to sell a vote you want
a receipt; you want some sort of proof of how you voted. This is why you don’t get receipt. You leave the election office and they just go, “Thank you for voting,”
or maybe put a sticker on your shirt saying you voted. They don’t give you any proof or confirmation of who you voted for. This is would be really handy; it would be
great to have receipts, if we had to do a recount. Everyone can poll their votes together and show who they voted for. But it has been understood for thousands of years that you
can’t do this. As soon as you provide receipts, you end up with massive electoral fraud and vote buy. This same situation, as I was trying to develop
some sort of electronic voting, can happen right here.
Say, this is your boss. You’re voting in your office, he can whisper, “Hey man vote for me, I’ll buy you some drinks”. “Vote for me, I’ll give you a raise”. Right
here he can see exactly who this guy voted for. Even though this guy in his head says, “My God, my boss is terrible”. But he is now in a position where not only
can he be intimidated but he can also sell his vote. So if he is thinking of making cash or getting that raise he will say, “Yeah, I’ll vote for you”. Bingo. Right there,
“Now give me the raise. I’d show you the vote.” Anytime you have someone who is voting and someone who is watching you have a problem.
That is why when you go to vote in a couple of days, you vote in person, in a private environment. You won’t have your husband there; you won’t have your boss there; you
won’t have your friend there. If the electoral committee is doing a good job they won’t let you go, “Hey, I just want to bring my friend with me while I vote.”
No friends allowed. You have to go alone. Of course here, there are all types and other forms of electoral fraud where you can hack in and change votes and all that. That’s
a problem in almost any electoral systems. That is something to watch out for whether you are voting in a booth or not. So, yeah you can have electoral fraud through hackers
but that does not change the necessity of someone voting privately, by themselves, no one can see how they voted. And what’s crazy is, I had to re-learn this.
I forgot about this when I was looking at electronic voting. It’s something that we should know. We teach secret ballots in the first grade. Here’s some first graders,
second graders, third graders, all voting with secret ballots, putting their folded votes in the box. High schoolers talk about it. Do projects on it. The secret ballot – why
it’s so great? How it began in the United States and completely took over.
Wikipedia nails it. They talk about this electoral fraud clearly. There’s no exceptions, right?
So here you have INTIMIDATION. Here you have VOTE BUYING. And here you have Wikipedia’s and everyone else’s solution at preventing this.
The secret ballot in which only the voter knows how individuals have voted is crucial part to ensuring free and fair elections. So it’s a crucial part for democracy because
if you do not have free and fair elections, you don’t have democracy.
Before the secret ballot it was common for candidates to intimidate, threaten, do whatever they could or bribe – buy votes. It was common. It was everywhere. The secret ballot
cured it. And again, as I hinted at before, it is not new. Aristotle was implementing ways to do a secret ballot 330 years before Christ was
born. These are some of the devices that Aristotle was playing with to make a secret ballot happen. And he discussed at length how to work this
process. So even if people were able to see someone voting they weren’t able to see how they voted. This was even before Aristotle. People were talking about secret voting in
Athens long before Aristotle. Our government agrees. There’s really no counter argument. Here’s Congressman John Kline, “Secret Ballot Protection Act.”
“Labor’s Loss: Secret Ballot, Protects the votes in Virginia.” And here's where they talk about a secret ballot. This would make it harder for labor leaders to intimidate
workers. Be it for joining a union, for joining anything, if you have a secret ballot intimidation is really, really difficult. There is no good
counter argument to the secret ballot, it’s just better. And that is why since the 1890’s, the United States and most of the world has upgraded.
They used to walk in and do a voice vote or used to say who they’re voting for but now everywhere we vote, everywhere I voted in my lifetime be it in a bake sale, the PTA,
it’s a secret vote. No husbands, no friends and no receipts. Private, only you know how
you voted. So everywhere we vote, we vote as private except for one place. In the U.S. government, in all of our democracy, there is one place
where secret voting does not happen. It almost as if we have this collective amnesia.
Everything in 1789 was open. We slowly changed everything. But we’ve forgotten to really deal with it in one particular place. Some of you already have guessed what this place
is – The U.S. Congress. The center of our democracy, the most vital
point of our democracy, votes in broad daylight; they vote in public. A lot of people are going, “That’s
great. I know how my congressman votes.” Well, we’re going to look at that and see the real problems with that idea. And…I’m sitting there in Uganda and I’m
thinking about this. I’m thinking about the absolute outrageousness of this. They’re hiding in broad daylight. They’re voting in public. Every single vote by a U.S. congressman
is tallied and publicized and put on online. And you can count every single one of them.
And we can just hop online govtrack.us and see how every congressman voted for everything.
Here’s Bradley, recent bill, he said yes. Here’s the people who voted against the bill. Every single congressman’s name in every single vote – public.
And sure, I mean, this happened back in the day right, they didn’t know any better.
So here we can go back to March 1st, 1799 look at any particular bill on the same website, we can see how each of our congressmen voted. There were lot fewer congressmen back then,
so here’s how they were seated. 13 to 17 against. We can see how this happened.
So we have a problem, right? We suggest that something happened in the 70’s. So is this my lionfish, if everyone had been voting this way all along? Is this
really the dramatic change that Robert Reich is talking about where we get enormous income inequality? Is this what Paul Ryan is suggesting the enormous increase in government expenditure?
Can we blame it on voting if this is the way that Congress always voted?
Well, maybe, we can because when I started to look at the 70’s, I didn’t have to go very far until I found this unknown bill. This is a bill you’ve never heard of. Certainly
one you’ve never read. This bill is called the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1970.
Okay, so “Legislative,” who is the legislative group? That is, the Congress. They are going
to reorganize how Congress does their stuff. It was proposed, sometime, I think, in April but it passed on October 26, 1970, effecting these changes.
And it’s really hard to find information about this act. It’s almost nothing. People say, “Oh this bill passed.” There are a little graphics showing some of the bill
but there is no discussion on this bill. This is going to be brand new to you. And this is going to be brand new to the public discourse about what happened in the 1970’s.
And here’s one quote though that is kind of interesting, “I thought the most significant anti-secrecy provision in the Act is the disclosure of house members’ votes in the Committee
of the Whole.” The Committee of the Whole is kind of this weird committee where Congress gets together, and in the old days before 1970, voted privately. So they did lots of
the Committees of the Whole to avoid public voting. But in 1970, that was changed.
Now, if you’re in the Committee of the Whole, your votes can and most likely will be recorded
and put on GovTrack.us; every single vote, every single congressman.
And so this quote elaborates, “The House often makes its most important policy decisions in that committee, but for 180 years its precedents had forbidden the recording of names in these
votes” -- private voting. They still did “yeas” and “nays” where they stood up and voted which isn’t very good, right? It’s still, as we know, needs to be private.
Secret ballot, no one knows how you voted. But for a “180 years, its precedents had forbidden the recording of these names in these votes.”
“Under the new rule in 1970, each member’s name and vote was to be recorded.” Seems
like such a subtle change; seems like might even be a good thing. To celebrate the event they also introduced this in January 23rd of 1973; it’s was like 800 thousand dollars
to install these electronic voting machines. Okay, because voting and actually doing roll call voting where you put the name next to the vote, even in 1970 after they passed the
bill; wasn’t used that much because it took so long.
So what they normally do is just have everyone get up who would say, “yea”; everyone get up saying, “nay” and they kind of go “Well, the ‘yeas’ are much bigger
than the ‘nays’, the bill’s passed.” If it was close, of course, they would start counting and they would count heads. But they wouldn’t record everyone’s name.
Now, because of this bill in 1970, they wanted to institute electronic voting so you could have votes that would be quick and precise; every single congressman’s name. So this
device would sit at their desk, they’d insert a card which identified them and then they would press their buttons yea, nay and then there’s other options but these are the
most common ones – green for yea, red for nay. Here are a couple of different pictures of the devices as they kind of change over the years.
As soon as they press yea or nay, this would be recorded, publicly. All the other senators,
all the other congressmen could see these votes and then they would get published online.
And I’m a big fan of our founding fathers, I thought they did an amazing job but they completely dropped the ball on voting procedures; they completely dropped the ball on secret
ballots. They didn’t talk about them. They didn’t institute them. They didn’t fully understand them. Even though Aristotle and others had been developing for a while it
just wasn’t currently in vogue in France and England where they were looking to build their democracy. And this as we’ll see has led to some problems.
Okay, so, it was acceptable to vote publicly in 1789. It was acceptable to walk in front of the sheriff and say whether you’re going to vote for the sheriff in 1789. But not now.
